lesson.title: Code on paper
lesson.subtitle: Strips, trace tables and desk checks

video.title: Code on paper: Strips, trace tables and desk checks
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.narration: The power went off for the whole of exam week, and my computing class still happened. Every pupil had a printed sheet: lines to put in order, a table to fill in, a bug to circle. We learned as much as with the phones.
Today: teaching and assessing code on paper.

Start with Parsons strips. Print a short program, cut it into lines, and add one distractor. Pairs put the strips in order on the desk, and draw the indents with a pencil. You can check twenty desks in two minutes.
Next, trace tables. Pupils copy a short program and draw a column for each variable. They go line by line, writing each new value in a new row. The last row shows what the program prints.

A desk check is a trace table for your own code or a partner’s, before you run it. Pupils write a program on paper, then trace it with two test inputs. If the table disagrees with what they expected, there’s a bug to find, with no device at all.

Paper is also a fair way to assess. Predict-the-output questions, Parsons strips and find-the-bug questions test understanding, not typing speed. Every pupil gets the same chance, with or without a phone at home.
Quick check! Trace it in your head. n starts at one and total at zero; while n is at most three, add n to total and add one to n. What does it print?
Six. A trace table makes it visible: one row each time round the loop, with n and total side by side. Pupils who answered ten forgot that the loop stops when n reaches four.

You don’t have to make all this from scratch. Every Darsi lesson has a printable worksheet. Its code questions come out as paper exercises: strips to number, gaps to fill, a line to circle, and the robot grid with cut-out cards.

Paper and phones work best together. Pupils predict and trace on paper, then one phone per group checks the answer. The phone becomes the judge, and the thinking stays on paper, where everyone can do it.

In the app, open Step through a program. Fill in a trace table on paper for A loop that adds, then press Next and check each row. Then change range of one, five to range of one, eleven, and predict the total before you run it.
Your turn. Half your class has no phone at home. Which homework is fairest?

Paper. Remember: Parsons strips, trace tables and desk checks teach real programming with no device. Paper is a fair way to assess. Darsi’s worksheets print the code steps for you. And one phone can be the judge.
Try it in class tomorrow: a paper-only lesson. Print the worksheet from this lesson’s kit, run it with pairs, and use one phone at the end to check the answers together.

checkpoints.prompt: n = 1, total = 0; while n <= 3: total = total + n, then n = n + 1. What is printed?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — total becomes 1, then 3, then 6, and the loop stops when n is 4.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — trace it: total is 1, 3, then 6; n reaches 4 and the loop stops.
